claims.text: Introducing a nanometric Y2O3 dispersion into a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve radiation tolerance.
The Y2O3 dispersion will not degrade high-temperature mechanical performance.
Mechanical alloying followed by consolidation can produce a uniform dispersion of approximately 1 vol% nanoscale Y2O3 in the alloy.
The dispersed Y2O3 particles create numerous oxide/metal interfaces that act as defect sinks.
Irradiation-generated vacancies and interstitials migrate toward the oxide/metal interfaces.
The Y2O3/metal interfaces will be coherent.
Vacancies and interstitials recombine at the oxide/metal interfaces.
Defect recombination at oxide/metal interfaces reduces irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Reduced defect accumulation lowers irradiation-induced swelling.
Reduced defect accumulation lowers radiation-induced embrittlement.
The Y2O3 nanodispersion provides oxide-dispersion strengthening.
Oxide-dispersion strengthening helps maintain high-temperature mechanical integrity.
The modified alloy will exhibit a lower density of radiation-induced defects than the unmodified baseline.
The modified alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced swelling or void formation than the unmodified baseline.
The modified alloy will retain hardness relative to the unmodified baseline after irradiation.
The modified alloy will retain tensile strength relative to the unmodified baseline after irradiation.
The beneficial effect is expected to hold during irradiation at approximately 600–800°C under fusion-relevant doses.
At substantially higher irradiation doses or temperatures, oxide-particle coarsening may diminish the beneficial effect.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires preservation or retention of mechanical performance, for which no statistically significant difference from the baseline would ordinarily be consistent. The falsification rule instead declares mechanical properties that are not significantly different from the baseline to be falsifying.
